title: Why does a patch still apply after the file has changed?
checkedAgainst: the Git on the machine (2.43.0 when this was written), which `model.test.ts` runs each time: its diff with one line of context must write the page's patch, and its apply, run verbosely, must place every hunk where the model does, say what the model says and leave the file the model leaves, on the page's four files, on a two-hunk patch whose second hunk is refused, and on 120 drifted copies of random files with one to three lines of context; `answers.ts` computes the check answers from the model. The search order was read from Git's apply.c at v2.43.0 and is held by those runs.

options.label: gained two lines at the top

answer: A hunk goes where its context and removed lines match the file; its line numbers only say where to look first

questions.question: Three lines are added above the author's file instead of two. Where does the hunk go, and which lines does Git try on the way?
questions.answer: At line 5, an offset of 3 lines. Git tries lines 2, 3, 1, 4 and 5: the line the header names, then one down, one up, two down, and, with nothing left above line 1, three down, where the hunk’s three old lines match.

questions.question: In the copy whose port was changed, the line the patch removes, workers = 2, is still there and unchanged. Why is the patch refused all the same?
questions.answer: Because the hunk expects 3 lines in a row: port = 8080, workers = 2 and timeout = 30. All of them must match, and with the port changed no 3 lines of the file do. Git tries lines 2, 3, 1 and 4, finds no match and reports the hunk’s own line, 2. The file is left untouched.

questions.question: The same change made with three lines of context is refused on the copy with two lines added at the top, though every line of the hunk is still in the file, in order. Why?
questions.answer: Its header is @@ -1,6 +1,7 @@, and a hunk that starts at line 1 is tried only at the top of the file: it claims to change the file’s first lines. With two new lines above them the top no longer matches, and Git looks nowhere else.

steps.title: A patch names lines to remove, lines to add, and lines to find
steps.line: Minus: remove. Plus: add. No mark: context, left alone.
steps.caption: This patch changes one setting in app.ini and adds another. Lines marked with a minus are removed and lines marked with a plus are added. The two unmarked lines are context: they are not changed, they are there so the change can be found. A block like this, context and all, is a hunk, and the line that starts @@ is its header.
steps.picture: The patch: --- a/app.ini / +++ b/app.ini / @@ -2,3 +2,4 @@ /  port = 8080 / -workers = 2 / +workers = 4 / +backlog = 64 /  timeout = 30; app.ini, numbered from 1: [web] / port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30 / [admin] / port = 9000.

steps.title: -2,3 says: 3 lines, starting at line 2
steps.line: The old side of a hunk is its context lines and its minus lines.
steps.caption: The header counts the hunk’s two sides. The old side is what the hunk expects to find: its context and minus lines, 3 lines starting at line 2 of the file. The brace marks them. The new side, +2,4, is what the hunk leaves: context and plus lines, 4 lines starting at line 2. These are line numbers in the author’s file, on the day the patch was made.
steps.picture: The patch: --- a/app.ini / +++ b/app.ini / @@ -2,3 +2,4 @@ /  port = 8080 / -workers = 2 / +workers = 4 / +backlog = 64 /  timeout = 30; app.ini, numbered from 1: [web] / port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30 / [admin] / port = 9000; The header @@ -2,3 +2,4 @@ is outlined and joined to a brace on the file’s lines 2 to 4, its old side. New in this step: The header @@ -2,3 +2,4 @@ is outlined and joined to a brace on the file’s lines 2 to 4, its old side.

steps.title: In the author’s file the hunk is where its header says
steps.caption: Git finds the 3 old-side lines at line 2, takes out the minus line and puts the plus lines in its place. This is the file the patch was made from, so everything is where the header says. But a hunk goes where its context and removed lines match the file; its line numbers only say where to look first. The next steps change the file under the patch to show it.

steps.title: Your copy has two new lines at the top
steps.line: Predict: will the patch still apply, and where?
steps.caption: The patch reaches you later, and your copy of app.ini has gained two lines at the top, so every line below them has moved down by two. The hunk still says line 2. Beside the file are the three lines it expects there, and the file’s lines 2 to 4 are not those. Will Git apply the patch at line 2, apply it at another line, or refuse it?
steps.picture: Your copy of app.ini, numbered from 1: ; settings / name = demo / [web] / port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30 / [admin] / port = 9000. Lines 1 and 2 are marked added; Beside the file, the three lines the hunk expects: port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30, level with line 2.

steps.title: Git tries lines 2, 3, 1 and 4 and finds the hunk at line 4
steps.line: From the line the header names: one down, one up, two down.
steps.caption: Git compares the hunk’s three old lines with the file at the line the header names, then one line down, one up, two down, working outward. At line 4 all three match, so that is where the hunk goes: an offset of 2 from where it was sent. The line numbers were only a first guess. What placed the hunk was its context.
steps.picture: Your copy of app.ini, numbered from 1: ; settings / name = demo / [web] / port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30 / [admin] / port = 9000. Lines 1 and 2 are marked added; Beside the file, the three lines the hunk expects: port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30, framed with the file’s lines from line 4. New in this step: Beside the file, the three lines the hunk expects: port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30, framed with the file’s lines from line 4.

steps.title: Applied at line 4, and Git says so only if asked
steps.caption: Git takes out the minus line and puts in the plus lines at line 4, as in the author’s file but two lines lower. Asked to be verbose, it reports the offset. Without -v it says nothing: a patch that applied at an offset looks like any other patch that applied.

steps.title: A patch can apply cleanly in the wrong place
steps.line: Git matched the lines. It cannot know which section was meant.
steps.caption: In this copy the [admin] section comes first and holds the same three lines. The hunk finds its old side at line 2 and Git applies it without a word: to [admin], though the author changed [web]. One line of context was too little to tell the sections apart. With the usual three, the hunk would have carried the [web] line itself and been refused. After applying a patch to a file that has changed, read the result.

steps.title: In your copy the port has changed
steps.line: Predict: will the patch still apply, and where?
steps.caption: The patch reaches you later, and in your copy someone has changed the port from 8080 to 8081. Nothing has moved: workers = 2, the line the patch removes, is still line 3. Beside the file are the three lines the hunk expects, starting at line 2. Will Git apply the patch at line 2, apply it at another line, or refuse it?
steps.picture: Your copy of app.ini, numbered from 1: [web] / port = 8081 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30 / [admin] / port = 9000. Line 2 is marked changed; Beside the file, the three lines the hunk expects: port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30, level with line 2.

steps.title: Git tries lines 2, 3, 1 and 4: the hunk fits nowhere
steps.line: From the line the header names: one down, one up, two down.
steps.caption: Git compares the hunk’s three old lines with the file at the line the header names, then one line down, one up, two down: every place three lines could go. Nowhere do all three match, because the context line port = 8080 is gone. The frame returns to line 2, the line Git will name. One changed context line refuses the hunk, though the line to remove is right there.
steps.picture: Your copy of app.ini, numbered from 1: [web] / port = 8081 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30 / [admin] / port = 9000. Line 2 is marked changed; Beside the file, the three lines the hunk expects: port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30, framed with the file’s lines from line 2. New in this step: Beside the file, the three lines the hunk expects: port = 8080 / workers = 2 / timeout = 30, framed with the file’s lines from line 2.

steps.title: Refused, and the file is left untouched
steps.caption: Git reports the hunk’s own line, 2, and stops. It writes nothing: had the patch held other hunks that fit, they would not be applied either. The outlined lines are the mismatch, port = 8081 in the file against port = 8080 in the hunk. To make this change, the patch has to be made again from the file as it is now, or the difference settled by hand.
